profile.intro: Hi, I'm Tina Wen, a student at the University of Michigan School of Information. I build data tools and interfaces, from power-market maps and AI data pipelines to research monitoring tools, and I care about the people who use them. Walk around the island to see my work, my projects, the places I've explored, and the communities I volunteer with.

items.title: Quantitative Developer Intern · Greenwich Commodities LLC
items.summary: Built data tools for power-market analysis across four projects, from mapping grid pricing nodes to an AI-powered pipeline that tracks U.S. data center development.

chapters.title: Mapping NYISO pricing nodes
chapters.text: Located the coordinates of NYISO pricing nodes so they could be shown on the firm's internal power-market map.

chapters.title: Converting SPP coordinates
chapters.text: Turned abstract x/y values into latitude and longitude with a third-degree polynomial model. I chose it after comparing several regression models, and it was validated against known locations. I also built an automated workflow that matches EIA generators to settlement locations.

chapters.title: Load and weather layers (PJM)
chapters.text: Built interactive map layers for county-level electricity load and six weather variables. The load layer flags unusual load against historical averages and can compare two time periods.

chapters.title: AI-powered data center tracker
chapters.text: Built a pipeline that collects news articles and extracts data center project details with LangExtract and the Gemini API, keeping each result tied to evidence in the source article. Results go through manual review and then feed a historical project table and an interactive dashboard.

items.sourceNote: Visuals are omitted to respect company confidentiality.

items.title: Project Manager | Data Analyst · American Library Association
items.kicker: FEB – MAR 2026 · CHICAGO, IL · UMSI ALTERNATIVE SPRING BREAK
items.summary: As project manager and data analyst on a UMSI student team, I helped ALA understand why members leave, turning 3,500+ survey records and a website UX review into a former-member survey and retention recommendations.

chapters.title: The challenge
chapters.text: ALA wanted to understand why members leave.

chapters.title: What we found
chapters.text: We analyzed 3,500+ membership survey records (2022–2025). Lapsed members showed three patterns: cost sensitivity, low perceived value, and limited awareness of benefits. A UX evaluation of the membership website found gaps in how benefits are shown and how information is organized, which may explain the low awareness.

chapters.title: The outcome
chapters.text: We designed a 19-question survey for former members covering pricing, benefit awareness and website findability. We presented it with targeted retention recommendations to ALA's Marketing and Community Engagement teams.

items.sourceNote: Team project through UMSI's Alternative Spring Break. My role: project manager and data analyst.

items.title: Michigan Ross Business+Tech Datathon · 3rd Place
items.kicker: FEB 2026 · ANN ARBOR, MI · TEAM LEADER | DATA ANALYST
items.summary: Led the construction-sector analysis for a team pitch that used 20 years of U.S. state GDP and tax data to recommend where to build a new manufacturing plant, finishing 3rd of 50 teams.

metrics.label: state GDP and tax data analyzed (through Q2 2025)

chapters.title: The question
chapters.text: Our cross-functional team analyzed U.S. state GDP and tax data from 2005 to Q2 2025 to answer an investment-style question: which state is the best place to build a new manufacturing plant? Each teammate owned one dimension: sales, construction, workforce, technology or supply chain.

chapters.title: My part: construction
chapters.text: I built the construction-sector ranking. It combines seven min–max normalized metrics in four groups: momentum (year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter growth), structural intensity (construction's share of GDP), scale (total and per-capita construction GDP) and resilience (volatility, and how well each state held up in 2020 compared with 2019).

chapters.title: The finding
chapters.text: We recommended Ohio not because it led any single dimension, but because it had no major weak spots: on our combined investment index it ranked 2nd in the Great Lakes region and 6th nationally. Turning that into a clear, audience-focused investment story helped us place 3rd of 50 teams.

items.sourceNote: Six-person team. I was team leader and owned the construction analysis.

items.title: Ann Arbor Data Dive (A2D2) · 1st Place
items.kicker: NOV 2025 · ANN ARBOR, MI · DATA ANALYST | TEAM MEMBER
items.summary: Analyzed Michigan campaign finance records to show how donor behavior changes over time, and presented the findings to the Michigan Department of State, winning 1st place.

metrics.label: place, for analytical depth and visualization
campaign finance records cleaned and integrated (2021–2025)

chapters.title: Preparing the data
chapters.text: Cleaned and integrated 200K+ Michigan campaign finance records (2021–2025) with NumPy and Pandas into a structured format for descriptive and comparative analysis.

chapters.title: What the data showed
chapters.text: Visualized donor-size concentration, spikes over time and gaps between candidates with Matplotlib and Seaborn. One striking pattern: in 2025, 67.2% of contributions were under $20, yet the small share of large donations brought in most of the money. The team also flagged 30 “donation dump” days across 9 campaigns, days when a committee received at least 50 donations and 5× its usual daily volume.

chapters.title: The outcome
chapters.text: Presented insights on campaign transparency and financial equity to the Michigan Department of State (MDOS), earning 1st place for analytical depth and visualization.

items.title: A Nature HCI Approach to Intergenerational Icebreaking · C&C ’25
items.kicker: JAN – APR 2025 · VIRGINIA TECH · SENIOR CAPSTONE · PUBLISHED JUNE 2025
items.summary: Our senior capstone study asked whether swapping short videos recorded in nature could help older and younger adults connect. It was published in the Proceedings of the 2025 ACM Conference on Creativity and Cognition (C&C ’25).

metrics.label: participants: 2 older adults (65+) and 4 younger adults

chapters.title: The question
chapters.text: Technology and nature are often treated as separate worlds, and bias between generations runs both ways. We asked whether asynchronous video storytelling in nature could break the ice between older adults (65+) and younger adults, and how tools for this could be designed better.

chapters.title: The study
chapters.text: For two weeks, two groups, each with one older adult and two younger adults, used the Marco Polo video app. On Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, members recorded 3–5 minute videos outdoors about what they saw or the memories it stirred; on Tuesdays and Thursdays, they replied to each other. We collected diary reflections, allophilia surveys (positive feelings toward the other age group) and semi-structured interviews, then ran a thematic analysis using the Jones et al. Nature HCI framework.

chapters.title: What we found
chapters.text: Storytelling in nature worked as an icebreaker. Places became triggers for memory (an apple tree brought back one participant's grandmother), and people lost track of clock time while talking about nature. These findings shaped design ideas for future tools: topic prompts to help people start a story, gentle ways to end a conversation instead of “ghosting,” and room for solitude alongside connection.

chapters.title: My role
chapters.text: I took part in the full two-week user study and wrote the first drafts of the Findings & Discussion and Design Implications sections. My teammates and our mentor then discussed and refined them with me. I also helped create our poster and give the presentation.

items.sourceNote: Four-person Virginia Tech team. I'm the second of four authors and drafted the findings and design implications.

chapters.title: The mission
chapters.text: The Hidden Figures group set out to highlight people from underrepresented groups in computing, starting with women in high-performance computing. My main job was the research: identifying about 150 women and gathering as complete a profile of each as I could.

chapters.title: Two ways to see their work

items.title: Breaking the Echo Chamber: Transforming the MHealthy Champion Network
items.kicker: SEP – DEC 2025 · ANN ARBOR, MI · UX RESEARCHER | TEAM MEMBER
items.summary: User research for MHealthy, U-M's workplace wellness program, which reaches employees through ~500 volunteer wellness champions. We found the real problem was a one-way feedback loop and proposed an AI workflow that gives champions department-specific reports.

metrics.label: solutions compared in a Pugh evaluation

chapters.title: Listening
chapters.text: Conducted semi-structured interviews with MHealthy leadership and a program coordinator as part of 6 stakeholder interviews, and synthesized the data through affinity mapping.

chapters.title: What we found
chapters.text: I wrote the Findings & Insights analysis, citing interview transcripts to surface 3 key insights: limited unit-level data, weak peer connections among champions, and systemic barriers to participation. The most surprising: MHealthy's data team already had participation data, but it never reached the coordinators and champions who needed it.

chapters.title: Reframing the problem
chapters.text: I helped reframe the problem from engaging shift workers to a one-way feedback loop: how might champions better understand the needs of the employees they represent? That led to 3 solutions compared in a Pugh evaluation. The top pick was an AI-powered workflow that turns cleaned participation data into ready-to-share, department-specific reports for champions.

items.sourceNote: Five-person team project for SI 500 at UMSI.

items.title: Halie & Co. Data Analysis · Alternative Fall Break
items.kicker: OCT 2025 · DETROIT, MI · DATA ANALYST | TEAM MEMBER
items.summary: Cleaned and analyzed inventory data for Halie & Co., a Detroit jewelry business, and turned the findings into purchasing and product recommendations.

chapters.title: Cleaning the inventory
chapters.text: Cleaned, standardized and merged the cabochon inventory datasets with NumPy and Pandas, harmonizing units and filling missing values to reach 100% schema consistency.

chapters.title: What the stones told us
chapters.text: Exploratory analysis with Matplotlib and Plotly showed blue as the clear favorite color and oval and round as the leading shapes, so we recommended deeper stock in those shapes and nearby shades like light blue and teal. Across the wider dataset, the team also found that sterling silver earned the highest profit margin (about 72%) despite moderate sales volume.

chapters.title: Better data next time
chapters.text: Proposed data-collection improvements, such as unique SKUs and standardized categories, so future analysis can go deeper.

items.sourceNote: Seven-person UMSI team through the Alternative Fall Break program.

items.title: Attendee · ACM Richard Tapia Celebration of Diversity in Computing
items.summary: I was selected from a competitive pool of scholarship applicants to represent Virginia Tech's underrepresented CS students at Tapia. Over the conference I met students and professionals from across computing and heard keynotes about building a career in tech. One highlight was a GenAI workshop: through hands-on activities, I explored what generative AI does well and what people still do better, which got me thinking about how to use it to work more efficiently without letting it replace me. I also went with a clear goal: to explore master's programs. That is where I first learned about the University of Michigan School of Information (UMSI). It shaped my decision to apply, and I'm now pursuing my master's there.

items.title: Millennium City Park
items.summary: A park that brings to life the Song dynasty capital painted in the famous scroll Along the River During the Qingming Festival. At night we watched Dongjing Menghua (“Dreams of the Eastern Capital”), a stunning show told through classical poetry. Through those poems, I watched the Song dynasty rise and fall.

items.summary: My whole family climbed Huangshan, the Yellow Mountains. The climb was exhausting, but seeing the famous Huangshan pines I had read about in my Chinese textbook was a real thrill.
